questions.question: Which method delivers the quickest kill?

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = x^2)
moves.professor: The derivative of the exponent is right there. One clean substitution ends the fight before it starts.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: IBP against a non-linear exponent will trap you in a loop. That's a swing at thin air.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution
moves.professor: There's no radical here. You're bringing a siege weapon to a dagger fight.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: Not a rational function. That blade shatters on impact.

questions.question: Choose the sharpest opening move for this integral.

moves.name: Complete the square, then use arctan formula
moves.professor: (x-3)^2 + 4 reveals an arctan hiding in plain sight. A single precise strike.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: Irreducible quadratic over reals. Your decomposition weapon can't even scratch this armor.

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = x^2 - 6x + 13)
moves.professor: du = 2x-6, but where's the x in the numerator? You stumble on the draw.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: No product in sight. IBP is a ghost swing here.

questions.question: What is the most efficient tactical decision here?

moves.name: Cancel common factor, then integrate
moves.professor: Factor out x: the enemy weakens to (x^2+1)/[x(x^2+1)] = 1/x. One clean stroke.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: You'd set up decomposition, but the common factor means you're just doing pointless work. A wasted attack.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution
moves.professor: No radical, no quadratic form. Wrong weapon entirely.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: Not a product of different function types. IBP has no hold here.

questions.question: What is the critical blow for this notorious integral?

moves.name: Integration by Parts (u = sec x, dv = sec^2 x dx)
moves.professor: The classic loop. IBP brings the integral back, then you isolate it. Surgical execution.

moves.name: Substitution u = tan x
moves.professor: You'll end up with a messier mix of roots and exponentials. This path leads straight into a trap.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution
moves.professor: No radical inside a trig function. You've lost sight of the battlefield.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: Not a rational function. That weapon can't even scratch this boss.

questions.question: Select the most lethal first move.

moves.name: Rewrite tan^3 as tan x(sec^2 x - 1), then split
moves.professor: One trig identity splits the enemy into two easy pieces. Swift and decisive.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: IBP with tan^3 alone leads nowhere. You'll waste precious time.

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = tan x) without rewriting
moves.professor: You're missing du = sec^2 x dx; the pieces don't fit. A clumsy swing.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution
moves.professor: No root of a quadratic. Wrong weapon, wrong fight.

questions.question: Which method clears the battlefield fastest?

moves.name: Substitution u = 4 - x
moves.professor: The radical becomes sqrt(u) and x becomes 4-u. Simple polynomial fight. Quick victory.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution (x = 4 sin^2 θ)
moves.professor: This also gets the job done, but you'll slog through extra trig. Not the cleanest path, but still a win.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: IBP with a radical? You'll sink into a swamp of fractional powers.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: A root in the numerator blocks any rational decomposition.

questions.question: Identify the correct weapon for this foe.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution (2x = 3 tan θ)
moves.professor: The form sqrt(u^2 + a^2) calls for tangent substitution. The whole thing collapses neatly.

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = 4x^2 + 9)
moves.professor: An extra x stays in the fight. You can't finish with that loose end.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: IBP doesn't know what to do with a radical in the denominator. Wasted energy.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: The square root blocks all rational attempts. This wall won't crack.

questions.question: What is the sharpest strategy against this even-powered enemy?

moves.name: Use power-reduction formulas (half-angle identities)
moves.professor: Both powers even? Lower the exponents until the enemy is just linear trig. Clean win.

moves.name: Separate a cosine for u-substitution
moves.professor: Both powers are even; you can't peel one off and leave an odd. Your blade glances off.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: Pure trig powers trap IBP in an endless loop with no exit.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution
moves.professor: No radical here. You've misread the entire skirmish.

questions.question: Choose the decisive strike for this radical foe.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution (x = 2 sin θ)
moves.professor: sqrt(a^2 - x^2) demands a sine substitution. The fight turns into a clean csc^2 encounter.

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = 4 - x^2)
moves.professor: You'll be left with an x that won't vanish. Ambush.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: The radical and x^2 combination defies IBP. You'll just exhaust yourself.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: The root blocks rational decomposition completely.

questions.question: What finishes this odd-powered trig foe quickly?

moves.name: Separate one sin, convert the rest to cosines, u = cos x
moves.professor: Odd power of sine? Peel one off and the remains become a polynomial in cos x. Swift kill.

moves.name: Use power-reduction formulas repeatedly
moves.professor: You can grind it down with half-angles. It'll work, but you'll sweat through many steps.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: Pure sine power traps IBP. You'll chase your own tail.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution
moves.professor: No radical. You've brought the wrong playbook.

questions.question: Identify the most efficient execution.

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = x^2 + 3x - 10)
moves.professor: The numerator is exactly the derivative of the denominator. One log and done.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: You can factor and decompose, but why take the long siege when the gate is open? Still works.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: Rational function not in product form. IBP cannot find a grip.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution
moves.professor: No radical means no trig sub. Misfire.

questions.question: Which tactic breaks the cycle?

moves.name: Integration by Parts twice, then solve for the integral
moves.professor: The classic boomerang. IBP brings back the original, and you isolate it. Perfectly executed.

moves.name: Use Euler's formula to convert to complex exponentials
moves.professor: An elegant flanking maneuver. Not the standard blade, but it lands the kill.

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = sin x)
moves.professor: e^x doesn't align with that substitution. You'll stumble into a deeper mess.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution
moves.professor: No square root of a quadratic. Wrong war.

questions.question: What is the best approach against this even power?

moves.name: Use power-reduction formulas (half-angle identities) twice
moves.professor: Lower that even power step by step until only linear trig remains. Flawless.

moves.name: Separate one cosine, convert the rest via sin^2
moves.professor: All powers are even; you can't steal one cos without leaving a fractional mess. Trap.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: Pure cos^4 triggers an infinite IBP loop with no resolution.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution
moves.professor: No radical. You're in the wrong battle.

questions.question: Choose the right substitution to dismantle this.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution (x = tan θ)
moves.professor: 1+x^2 under a 3/2 power is a tan sub beacon. The radical becomes sec^3, and the fight simplifies.

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = 1 + x^2)
moves.professor: You'll have an extra x and no way to handle the power elegantly. Stuck.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: The rational-like form resists IBP. Your weapon bounces off.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: Not a polynomial denominator. That blade shatters.

questions.question: Which opening gambit wins this cleanly?

moves.name: Polynomial long division, then integrate
moves.professor: Improper fraction? Divide and get x - x/(x^2+1). Two simple integrals. Done.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution (x = tan θ)
moves.professor: This works, turning it into tan^3, but you'll fight extra trig identities. Not optimal, but victorious.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: Improper degree means partial fractions cannot be applied directly. You'll crash at the first step.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: Not a product of different types. IBP has no hold.

questions.question: What is the most direct route to victory?

moves.name: Integration by Parts (u = arcsin x, dv = dx)
moves.professor: A lone inverse trig function: u is the function, dv=dx. IBP turns it into an algebraic fight.

moves.name: Substitution x = sin θ
moves.professor: You get ∫ θ cos θ dθ, which still needs IBP. A detour, but you'll reach the target.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution
moves.professor: No radical of a quadratic. You've misidentified the enemy.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: Not a rational function. This weapon is useless.

questions.question: Pick the tactic that ends this cleanly.

moves.name: Use product-to-sum identity
moves.professor: Different frequencies in sine and cosine? Product-to-sum splits it into easy integrals. One strike.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: IBP will cycle the products endlessly. You'll exhaust yourself.

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = sin(3x) or cos(2x))
moves.professor: Derivatives don't match. A clumsy swing that leaves you exposed.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution
moves.professor: No radical. Wrong battlefield.

questions.question: Which opening blow is most lethal?

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = x^3)
moves.professor: x^2 dx is exactly one-third du. One substitution, one clean sine. Perfect.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: The cosine of x^3 defies IBP. You'll get nowhere fast.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution
moves.professor: No square root. Wrong weapon.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: Not a rational function. This blade snaps.

questions.question: Which method dispatches this foe most efficiently?

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: Denominator factors into (x-2)(x+2). Decompose and get two logs. Quick and decisive.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution (x = 2 sec θ)
moves.professor: That route works, but you'll wade through trig to get the same log result. A longer path.

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = x^2 - 4)
moves.professor: du = 2x dx, but no x in the numerator. You're swinging at shadows.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: No product to separate. IBP dead on arrival.

questions.question: Find the surest path through this mixed foe.

moves.name: Complete the square, then split into two integrals
moves.professor: (x+1)^2+1 appears. Split into something over the quadratic plus a constant over the quadratic; one yields ln, the other arctan.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution (x+1 = tan θ)
moves.professor: Also works, but forces you through extra trig. You get the kill, but it's slower.

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = x^2 + 2x + 2)
moves.professor: The numerator x doesn't match du = 2x+2. Can't close the strike.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: Irreducible denominator. Decomposition is impossible here.
